To intimate something means to make it known in an indirect, subtle way — to hint at it rather than state it openly and directly.

When you intimate something, you are not announcing it with clear, plain words. You are allowing the other person to understand something through careful suggestion — through a gently chosen phrase, a tone of voice, a meaningful look, or a remark that points toward something without naming it. The message still reaches the listener. They understand what you mean. But you never said it out loud in straightforward language.
A simple example to feel the word:

Imagine a teacher who is reviewing a student's essay. Instead of saying "This essay is not good enough," the teacher says, "I wonder if there's still room to push this piece a little further." The student understands: the essay needs more work. The teacher has intimated that the essay is not yet up to standard, without bluntly saying so.

Another example: A friend is visiting your house, and after a long evening you say, "Well, it's getting quite late, isn't it?" You haven't asked them to leave. But you have intimated that it's time to wrap up.
The most important thing to understand about this word:

The indirectness in "intimate" is deliberate. You are not being vague because you are confused or unsure. You are choosing to communicate sideways rather than head-on. People intimate things for many reasons — because the subject is sensitive or awkward, because bluntness would seem rude in that setting, because they want to protect themselves (after all, you can't be held fully accountable for something you never actually said directly), or simply because the situation calls for a gentler, more delicate touch.
How it differs from similar words (this is important):

"To intimate" sits in a family of words that all involve indirect communication, but each one is slightly different.

To hint is the closest everyday equivalent. "Intimate" is simply the more formal, sophisticated version of "hint." If you say "she hinted," it feels casual. If you say "she intimated," it feels elevated and precise — the kind of word you'd find in a novel or a formal piece of writing.

To imply is about what is embedded within the words you actually use. If you say "The food here used to be better," you imply — without saying — that the food has gotten worse. It's about what your sentence naturally carries inside it. "Intimate" puts more focus on the speaker consciously choosing to communicate something in a delicate, understated way.

To insinuate also means to suggest something indirectly, but it almost always carries a negative or suspicious flavor — you insinuate that someone did something wrong, or has an ulterior motive. "Intimate" is neutral. You can intimate pleasant things, neutral things, or bad things. Insinuate is nearly always used for something unflattering.

To allude means to reference something without naming it directly. "She alluded to her difficult childhood" — she referred to it without going into it fully. With "allude," the focus is on reference and mention. With "intimate," the focus is on actually conveying or communicating something to the listener — making them understand it.
How it is used in real sentences:

"The doctor intimated that the recovery would take longer than first expected." (He suggested it carefully, without giving a direct prognosis.)

"During the meeting, the director intimated that budget cuts were coming." (She didn't announce it officially, but the signal was there.)

"He intimated his disapproval with a long silence and a slow shake of his head." (Sometimes intimating doesn't even require words.)

"The letter intimated that their offer was final and no further negotiations would be entertained." (A formal, written example — the letter's tone made it clear without stating it harshly.)

"Intimate" used as a verb is a formal word. You would not typically use it in casual conversation with friends. You are far more likely to encounter it in literature, journalism, formal speeches, legal contexts, or careful writing. In everyday speech, people simply say "hint" or "suggest." But knowing this word allows you to both understand it when you read it and use it with precision when the moment calls for it.
One common trap — do not confuse it with "intimidate."

These two words look and sound somewhat similar, but they mean entirely different things. To intimidate someone is to make them feel frightened or threatened — to use fear as a form of pressure. To intimate something is to communicate it subtly and indirectly. They are not related in meaning at all. The similarity is only in appearance.
The complete picture in one sentence:
To intimate is to let something be understood — quietly, carefully, and without saying it outright — by leaving just enough of a signal that the thoughtful listener can fill in the rest themselves.
